planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Topsy Turvy echeveria holds its curled leaf form and powdery coating best in bright light and rots in wet soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Topsy Turvy echeveria holds its curled leaf form and powdery coating best in bright light and rots in wet soil. Thick, powdery, silvery-blue leaves curl sharply backward and inward toward the stem, an unusual, almost folded-under shape that gives the rosette a wavy, sculptural silhouette unlike the flat, open rosettes of most other echeverias. Its striking, unmistakable form and cool blue-gray color make it a favorite for succulent arrangements and collector displays, and it offsets over time to form small clusters. Water only when the soil is fully dry, avoid wetting the leaves to protect the delicate powdery bloom, and provide bright light to keep the rosette tight and well-colored.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Gollum jade plant is extremely drought-tolerant and rots quickly in wet or dense soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Gollum jade plant is extremely drought-tolerant and rots quickly in wet or dense soil. Thick, tubular, jade-green leaves curl into narrow, trumpet-like tubes with a distinctive suction-cup-shaped, reddish-tinged tip, a quirky, novelty form of the classic jade plant that branches into a sturdy, tree-like miniature shrub over time. Sometimes sold and grown as bonsai material for its naturally gnarled, woody branching habit, it is just as easy-care and forgiving of neglect as the standard jade plant, tolerating irregular watering and low humidity typical of most homes. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for the best leaf color and compact form, and prune to shape as the plant matures into a small, tree-like specimen.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Hobbit jade plant is extremely drought-tolerant and rots quickly in wet or dense soil.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Hobbit jade plant is extremely drought-tolerant and rots quickly in wet or dense soil. Glossy green leaves curl into tight tubes that partially overlap and cluster densely along thick stems, similar to the related 'Gollum' cultivar but more tightly curled and closely spaced, giving the plant an even bushier, more clustered look. It shares the standard jade plant's easy care, tolerating low humidity, irregular watering, and general neglect while slowly developing thick, woody, tree-like stems that make it a popular subject for succulent bonsai. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for compact, well-colored growth, and repot every few years into a slightly larger container as the woody stem thickens.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; felt bush is a large-growing Madagascar succulent shrub that needs excellent drainage and tolerates full sun once acclimated.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; felt bush is a large-growing Madagascar succulent shrub that needs excellent drainage and tolerates full sun once acclimated. Large, undulating, triangular leaves are covered in a dense, brown-gray, velvety felt of fine hairs, giving the foliage a soft, suede-like texture and grayish color that is dramatically different from the smooth, glossy leaves of most kalanchoes, with the cultivar 'Fang' developing curious tooth-like growths on the leaf undersides. Left to grow, it becomes a substantial architectural shrub well over head height in frost-free gardens, or a striking large container specimen elsewhere, contrasting bold, felted texture against finer-leaved succulent companions. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright light for compact, well-textured growth, and protect from any frost.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Penwiper Plant tolerates somewhat lower light than many succulents but colors and flowers best with bright light.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to partial sun in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Penwiper Plant tolerates somewhat lower light than many succulents but colors and flowers best with bright light. Broad, rounded, pale gray-green leaves are boldly marked with large, irregular, purplish-brown blotches, a striking mottled pattern that gives the plant its whimsical common name from a supposed resemblance to a stained cloth used for wiping pens. Native to Ethiopia and East Africa, it produces clusters of white, waxy, fragrant flowers on tall stems in winter, a welcome bloom period when few other succulents are flowering. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright indirect to full light for the boldest leaf markings, and propagate easily from leaf or stem cuttings.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; short-leaved aloe is compact, cold-tender, and clusters readily into a tidy mat over time.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; short-leaved aloe is compact, cold-tender, and clusters readily into a tidy mat over time. Thick, triangular, pale blue-gray leaves edged with small white teeth form a tight, dense rosette that offsets freely at the base, quickly forming a low, clumping mat, with spikes of coral-orange, tubular flowers rising well above the foliage in spring, attracting hummingbirds where grown outdoors. Native to South Africa's Western Cape, it is one of the smaller, more compact aloe species commonly grown, making it well suited to a succulent dish garden, rock garden pocket, or mixed container where larger aloes would be out of scale. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide full sun for the best blue coloring, and separate offsets to propagate or control spread.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; fairy washboard tolerates lower light than sun-loving succulents and scorches in direct hot sun.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; fairy washboard tolerates lower light than sun-loving succulents and scorches in direct hot sun. Thick, dark green triangular leaves are ridged with raised, corrugated, washboard-like horizontal ribs, an intricate textured pattern that spirals up the tightly packed rosette and gives the plant its distinctive common name. Native to rocky grasslands in South Africa, it is a slow-growing, clustering species well suited to a succulent dish garden or windowsill collection where its unusual ribbed texture is easy to appreciate up close. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide bright but indirect light to avoid scorching, and separate offsets from the base to propagate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Horse's Teeth wants excellent drainage above all else and rots quickly if the soil stays damp.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded xeriscape container in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; Horse's Teeth wants excellent drainage above all else and rots quickly if the soil stays damp. Thick, gray-green leaves are abruptly cut off flat at the tip as if sheared with scissors, arranged in two opposite rows rather than a spiraling rosette, an extraordinarily unusual growth form among succulents that mimics the plant's natural habit of growing nearly buried in gritty soil with only the flat, translucent-edged leaf tips exposed to filter light. Native to the Eastern Cape of South Africa, it is a slow-growing collector's succulent best displayed in a shallow pot where its odd, architectural form and two-ranked leaf arrangement can be fully appreciated. Water only when the soil is completely dry, plant slightly deeper than typical succulents to mimic its natural partly-buried habit, and provide bright but indirect light.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
